Wallow

/WAH-loh/ - rhymes with hollow · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Wallow means to remain helplessly sunk in an emotion or state.

Weeks after the contest, Priya still wallowed in the loss, keeping the silver medal face-down and retelling the final round every night.

Worked Example

The self-help chapter draws the line between grieving and wallowing: grief moves, even slowly, while the wallower circles — same complaints, same couch, same soundtrack, the misery kept warm because at least it is familiar.

Wallow began with pigs rolling in mud, and the picture holds: to wallow in self-pity or guilt is to settle into the feeling and stay, half-helpless and half-comfortable. The word always carries a raised eyebrow — it says you could climb out.

How Wallow Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

languish

languish: to droop and fade in a bad state — passive, where wallowing is indulgent

mope

mope: to drift about listlessly; wallowing digs in and stays

Antonyms

rally

rally: to pull yourself together and fight back

recover

recover: to climb back to normal after the blow

How Strong Is It? — dwell → mope → wallow

dwell vs. wallow

dwell vs. wallow: Dwelling on a setback is far milder than wallowing in it — your thoughts keep returning, but life goes on.

mope vs. wallow

mope vs. wallow: Moping is weaker than wallowing — a mope droops and sighs for an afternoon, while wallowing means settling into the misery and staying.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — wallow

Root — wallow: to roll about (Old English wealwian)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: wallow is Old English wealwian, 'to roll about,' in one piece. Picture a pig rolling luxuriously in cool mud — that literal wallowing is still the word's first sense, and the emotional sense simply moves the mud indoors: rolling around in a feeling instead of getting up.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Wealwian never spawned an English family — wallow climbed out of the sty alone. Its only kin are distant ancient cousins that took other roads into the language, so the pig in the mud remains the whole story, and the best possible memory hook.

Strength Check

Word Choice

informal, disapproving

Wallow accuses: it says someone is staying in the mud of a feeling because climbing out takes effort — wallowing in self-pity, in guilt, in nostalgia. Mope is gentler, mere listless drifting; languish is passive fading. Wallowing is a choice, made daily, and the word never lets you forget it. It keeps its preposition too: you wallow IN something.
